claim_grade: Video: D-claim, Tier 2 (educational channel; host is a credentialed economist but the piece is a commercial, Economist-sponsored explainer, not peer-reviewed, and its headline number is misdescribed). Posted 8 October 2026 (YouTube uploadDate 2026-10-08T05:30 PDT), runtime 21:13; 257,756 views and 4,653 likes when fetched on 14 October 2026 (the queue's '249K' and '9 October' are slightly stale/off). The on-screen host speaks in the first person ('in our research', 'I did see...' in Seoul). Schasfoort is an economist associated with the University of Groningen (agent-based macro modelling; a 2017 Advances in Complex Systems paper per RePEc/INET listings); whether his PhD is completed was not confirmed from an official profile, though the channel styles him 'Dr.'. content_summary.what_98_percent_refers_to: The video says (00:00:58-00:01:11, auto-caption): 'according to a University of Chicago survey, 98% of economists that had an opinion on the matter agreed that a land value tax would be a great idea.' It does not name the survey on screen or in prose, but source 5 in the description is kentclarkcenter.org/surveys/land-value-tax/, i.e. the IGM/Clark Center Economic Experts Panel poll 'Land Value Tax', dated 2 November 2023. The poll statement (paraphrased; verbatim is 51 words): shifting municipal property tax from buildings towards land, as in Detroit's plan, will enhance owners' incentives to develop and thereby give a substantial boost to local economic growth over a ten-year horizon.
content_summary.poll_figures_from_primary: Panel: 41 US panelists. Raw votes tallied from the panelist list on the page: Strongly agree 3, Agree 19, Uncertain 7, Disagree 1 (Richard Thaler), No opinion 1 (David Autor), Did not answer 10. Raw percentages in the page data: 7.3 / 46.3 / 17.1 / 2.4 / 0 / 2.4 / 24.4 of the 41. Confidence-weighted (the Clark Center's headline chart): Strongly agree 13%, Agree 70%, Uncertain 14%, Disagree 2%, Strongly disagree 0% (page data array weightedPV7634_0). Reconstruction (T0 inference, not stated by either source): '98%' is most plausibly 100% minus the 2% weighted 'Disagree', i.e. the share of confidence-weighted votes that did NOT disagree, which includes the 14% 'Uncertain'. Weighted agreement is about 83%; among panelists casting any substantive vote (30), 22 agree (73%); excluding 'Uncertain', 22 of 23 agree (96%). Qualifying comments on the page: Thaler (the lone Disagree) says 'substantial' overstates the effect because land's market value in Detroit is low; Schmalensee 'agree with the direction of the effect but choke on "substantial"'; Duffie 'Directionally, yes'; Acemoglu 'More generally, Georgist ideas may be worth revisiting.' (all page comments, short). The video's other named supporters (Friedman, Stiglitz, Krugman) are not among the 41 panelists, so the poll does not document their views; Friedman's 'least bad tax' is already carried on concepts/land-value-tax.md from a primary.
content_summary.what_the_video_otherwise_says: Standard explainer content: Henry George history, land fixed so no deadweight loss, split-rate shift cuts building tax and raises land tax, Cincinnati modelling by the Center for Land Economics (Tier 2 partner), Pittsburgh/Denmark/Estonia/Australian states, Kentucky and Virginia 2026 enabling laws (already covered at events/2026-state-lvt-enablement-wave.md), 1910 People's Budget valuation problem, Korea representative-plots method, and the host's own conclusion that LVT 'can absolutely help' but is not a magic bullet without zoning reform and public housing. Nothing here is a new primary finding. The video explicitly says (about 00:12:36-00:13:11) that the empirical studies of LVT are thin and 'suffer from a lack of reliable data', which is consistent with the wiki's cautious grading.

The wedge result itself is standard public-finance theory (C-claim) that has Tier 1 backing already on the wiki (Mirrlees Review at concepts/deadweight-loss.md source 1; Cao et al. 2015); what is Doucet's is the framing and the pencils/parcels contrast.

content_summary.the_argument: Target: a critique that LVT advocates conflate the amount of land that exists with the amount offered to the market, and that Econ 101 sales-tax analysis shows the offered amount falls under a tax. Method: apply two taxes, a sales tax (10% of pre-tax selling price) and a holding tax (a recurring annual tax on the market value of every unit that exists, assumed as easy to observe as land), to a produced asset (pencils) and a non-produced asset (land). Pencils, sales tax: buyer pays $1.10, seller gets $1.00, a 'wedge'; deadweight loss from forgone trades; existing stock sells through more slowly; marginal producers exit, so future stock shrinks. Pencils, holding tax: no wedge (buyer and seller trade at the same, lower price); the tax is capitalised once into a lower price borne by whoever holds the asset at enactment; holders offload or destroy pencils they do not need, so the amount OFFERED rises; low-margin producers still exit, so the long-run stock falls; hence 'Both taxes introduce deadweight loss through the loss of future production' but only the sales tax adds a wedge. Land, sales tax (a transfer tax / stamp duty): same wedge and less offered, 'significant deadweight loss, even though land is non-produced and its supply is fixed'; he cites a German estimate of 67 euro cents of deadweight loss per 100 raised (linked: CESifo Working Paper 6321). Land, holding tax: no wedge; amount offered increases because the liability bites 'no matter what is done with the land or who owns it'; idle holders of valuable land face the strongest incentive to sell; unlike pencils nobody can destroy land, so 'Who holds land changes, but not whether it's held', making reallocation neutral at worst and beneficial when land moves from idle speculators to users; capitalisation into a lower price is a one-time loss to the holder at announcement. Concession: 'Critics are right to point out that the Econ 101 textbook supply curve refers to the amount offered for sale', but 'land value tax is not a sales tax, but a holding tax'. Caveat he states: untaxing buildings raises land prices and may offset the capitalisation effect of a higher land tax, 'beyond the scope of this article'; holding taxes 'are not magical' and can still be destructive on produced assets.
content_summary.role_of_non_produced_rival_necessary_loc: 'Non-produced' is the efficiency hinge: it removes the production margin, so neither stock nor future supply responds to either tax. 'Rival', 'necessary' and 'locational' are not used in the wedge argument; they are the stated reasons (alongside 'others') why LVT advocates single out this holding tax: a rival asset (one person's ownership excludes another), a necessary asset (everyone must access it to exist) and a locational asset that 'passively obtains value from the labor and investment of its neighbors'. They carry the fairness/justification case, not the zero-deadweight-loss case.

content_summary.series_context: Part 1 (reclamation / Netherlands) argued that reclaimed land is an improvement on previously useless submerged land and that LVT advocates mean 'location'; Part 3 will address the value-versus-amount dispute (owners lowering land value to cut tax, e.g. NIMBYism or dumping waste, building up, search and entitlement costs). Reader comments on the page (two visible) are not citable; one notes that deadweight loss does not by itself imply value destruction if government money is worth more than private money.
content_summary.what_it_adds_beyond_existing_pages: concepts/deadweight-loss.md states the zero-deadweight-loss result as a consequence of fixed supply and never states or answers the 'amount offered versus amount in existence' objection; it says 'its quantity is fixed regardless of price' without distinguishing the stock from the quantity offered. The post supplies (a) a plain statement of that objection, (b) the concession that the offered quantity responds to price, (c) the rejoinder that the result rests on the tax being a holding tax with no wedge, not on supply elasticity of offered units, and (d) a worked sales-tax versus holding-tax contrast. It adds no new empirical evidence and no new theorem; it is a pedagogical restatement of standard wedge logic by a Tier 2 proponent. The only data point, the German transfer-tax estimate (Büttner, CESifo WP 6321, 2017, abstract: 'about 67 cents' of additional deadweight loss per extra euro of revenue), is a Tier 1 comparator that the wiki lacks and that pairs naturally with the Treasury/Cao et al. 72 cents for conveyancing stamp duty already on concepts/deadweight-loss.md.
suggested_enrichment_sentences: concepts/deadweight-loss.md (new paragraph after 'Why Land Value Tax Has Zero Deadweight Loss', under an attributed heading such as 'The "Amount Offered" Objection'): 'A common objection is that the relevant supply in textbook tax analysis is the quantity offered for sale, not the quantity in existence, and that the offered quantity does respond to price and to taxes. The practitioner-author and proponent Lars Doucet (2026) accepts the premise but argues it does not reach a recurring tax on holding land: a sales or transfer tax opens a wedge between buyer's and seller's prices and reduces the amount offered, whereas a holding tax opens no wedge and, he argues, increases the amount offered, because land cannot be destroyed and can only change hands.' (Cite the post as origin/proponent only; D-claim.)

(B-claim, working paper; cite CESifo WP 6321. Confirm author and sample from the PDF before publishing; the abstract page fetched does not list the author.)

concepts/land-value-tax.md ('Why Land Supply Is Inelastic', one sentence): 'Critics note that what is offered for sale can vary even though the stock of land cannot; proponents reply that a recurring holding tax, unlike a transfer tax, creates no price wedge on the units offered.' Link to deadweight-loss for the attribution.

Sources entry: Tier 2, D-claim, cite progress.org for Part 1 and the Substack for Part 2.

existing_wiki_coverage: Searched: grep of concepts/objections/research/benefits/problems/narratives for 'land supply', 'supply of land', 'fixed supply', 'perfectly inelastic', 'amount offered', 'reclaim', plus the digest. No page states or answers the 'offered versus existing' objection or cites the series. concepts/deadweight-loss.md (last_reviewed 2026-07-16): zero-deadweight-loss section rests on 'perfectly inelastic' land supply; carries Smith 1776, Pigou 1920, the Gaffney 2005 attributed critique of Harberger-triangle measurement, Gross & Klein 2026, and Cao et al. 2015 (marginal excess burden: stamp duty 72 cents, company tax about 50, flat labour tax 21, broad land tax minus 10) plus Dobes et al.; no transfer-tax study outside Australia and no mention of the Büttner RETT paper (the wiki's research/buettner-german-land-tax-capitalization.md is a different Büttner paper). concepts/land-value-tax.md 'Why Land Supply Is Inelastic' (lines 22-24): states inelasticity flatly, in two sentences, with no objection or reply. research/gaffney-excess-burden-shiftable-taxes.md: Gaffney's alternative excess-burden metric (land-use shifting), attributed. research/doucet-does-georgism-work.md: Parts 1-3 of the 2021-22 ACX series and the September 2026 'Five Years Later' post (Tier 2, navigation source); no mention of the 2026 land-supply series. people/lars-doucet.md and organizations/center-for-land-economics.md exist. objections/laffer-curve-applies-to-lvt.md and objections/land-is-just-capital.md rely on fixed supply without the offered-quantity distinction. The syndicated Part 1 (https://www.progress.org/articles/is-land-supply-fixed-part-1-the-netherlands-and-land-reclamation/) is cited nowhere on the wiki; the only occurrence of the series' URLs in the repository is sources/wiki-queue.json. The Netherlands/reclamation topic has no coverage (grep 'land reclamation', 'polder': only an unrelated Dutch polder-maintenance exemption on research/lincoln-institute-past-forward-property-tax-history.md).
uncertainties: Part 3 is unpublished, so the series' answer to the value-versus-amount dispute (the objection that owners can lower land value to cut tax) is unknown; no verdict on the series as a whole should be final.

The post's claim that a holding tax increases the amount offered is a theoretical prediction; it is not tested against data in the post, and in practice assessment error or taxes that fall partly on improvements (ordinary property tax) can reintroduce margins Doucet's stylised holding tax assumes away.

Büttner (2017) author attribution comes from a search of RePEc/CESifo listings, not from the fetched ifo abstract page; the 67-cent figure and wording are from that fetched abstract. The post says 'real estate transfer taxes in Germany' and the paper's preferred estimate is a marginal figure (per additional euro), which the post paraphrases as 'for every 100 raised'.

The post's date is 13 October 2026 (page metadata) and the blog URL domain differs from the queue's older Substack naming; the same text may also be available at progressandpoverty.substack.com. The wiki's other 2026 Doucet pieces cite blog.landeconomics.org.
Whether T1 wants a series page after Part 3 is an editorial call; the delta rule used elsewhere (no new page for a restatement without new evidence) argues for ENRICH only.

tier1_primaries_found: ATO Corporate Tax Transparency, PRRT data: payable $1,996.6m (2021-22), $1,867.1m (2022-23, 11 entities), $1,483.3m (2023-24, 16 entities), $1.87bn (2024-25, 21 entities; +26.3%, +$389.6m on the prior year, 'mainly driven by' entities paying under the deductions cap; page published 1 October 2026).

ATO PRRT deductions cap: entity 'taken to have a taxable profit of 10% of the assessable receipts' where the cap applies (qualifying LNG projects, excluded for the first financial year of receipts and the following 7); 'applies from 1 July 2023'; the instalment regime for the cap applies from years beginning on or after 1 July 2024. ATO new-legislation page: enacted as Schedule 5 of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Accountability and Fairness) Act 2024, taking effect 1 July 2023; deductions limited to 90% of assessable receipts per project interest; disallowed amounts carried forward and uplifted at the long-term bond rate; purpose 'bring forward PRRT receipts from LNG projects'.

Budget Paper No. 1 2026-27 (12 May 2026), Statement 5, Table 5.7 cash receipts: PRRT $1,420m (2024-25 actual), $1,400m (2025-26), $1,900m (2026-27), $1,750m, $1,550m, $1,250m (2029-30); text: revised up $400m in 2026-27 and $1.6bn over 2025-26 to 2029-30 since MYEFO because of the Middle East conflict oil price and volumes; Table 5.5 shows the 2025-26 figure revised down $100m from MYEFO ($1,500m to $1,400m).
DISR Office of the Chief Economist, Resources and Energy Quarterly December 2025: LNG export earnings forecast to fall from $65bn in 2024-25 to $47bn by 2026-27.

Senate Select Committee on the Taxation of Gas Resources (established 30 March 2026; report due 7 May 2026): chapter 1 records over 230 submissions and three hearings (21, 22, 24 April 2026), found that lack of timely, transparent entity-level data makes revenue, profits and PRRT liabilities hard to assess, and could not agree recommendations (views in additional comments). ATO evidence to the committee (Assistant Commissioner Suzie Emery, Hansard 22 April 2026 p.63, quoted via Pocock/Greens comments): carry-forward expenditure of $282.6bn as at 2023-24; total assessable receipts of all PRRT projects $46.18bn in 2023-24 against about $1.5bn PRRT collected (roughly 3%, derived). Treasury evidence (Marty Robinson, 22 April 2026 p.63): with exports under long-term or spot global-price sales, the burden of an export tax 'would be more likely to fall on the producers' (second-hand via committee comments). Labor senators: Recommendation 1 (Treasury or Productivity Commission report on petroleum revenue and tax paid) and 2 (modelling of reform proposals after the Middle East crisis); Treasury forecasts $5.4bn PRRT over four years; combined marginal rate once PRRT bites 54-58%. Coalition senators cite ATO transparency data of $10.4bn oil-and-gas company tax in 2023-24.

Senate Economics Committee report on the 2023 deductions-cap bill, chapter 3: Treasury officials said the 90% cap guarantees upfront payments and was 'carefully considered' not to deter investment; the committee found it 'strike[s] the right balance'; Australia Institute argued the cap holds revenue steady in nominal terms only. Treasury 2023 Review of PRRT Gas Transfer Pricing Arrangements (7 May 2023) and the 2017 Callaghan Review are cited in the committee comments (not fetched).
comparison_with_existing_pages: research/australia-mining-royalties-prrt.md says the 2023 reform 'capped annual deductions at roughly 90% of assessable receipts, effective 1 July 2024'. That date is wrong: the cap applies from 1 July 2023 (ATO); 1 July 2024 is when the cap's instalment regime began, and the legislation passed in 2024 (which is the likely origin of the error and of the ABC's 'amended the tax in 2024'). The sentence also says the reform front-loaded collections 'without raising the total lifetime tax take'; the ATO and Treasury describe it as bringing forward receipts, so this is consistent but unsourced.

The same page's PRRT mechanics, royalty rates and the 2023/2024 reform rest on kurums.com, a business-intelligence explainer the page itself flags as unverified against ATO/Treasury/state sources (its 'Nuances and Limits' section); the primaries above now verify the 40% rate, the cap, its 10% deemed-profit mechanics and the date, and can replace that source for those claims. Its $282bn carried-forward figure (from Diane Kraal, The Conversation, Aug 2026) is corroborated by the ATO evidence ($282.6bn at 2023-24).

research/nassios-australia-lng-prrt-structural-limits.md (CoPS WP G-372, 2026) gives PRRT revenue of A$1.5bn (2014) rising to A$2.3bn (2023) and a ~15% capture rate. The ATO payable series puts 2022-23 at $1,867.1m and 2023-24 at $1,483.3m, so the A$2.3bn does not reconcile with ATO payable (possibly a cash-receipts or calendar-year measure; check Nassios's data note). It also predates the 2024-25 jump to $1.87bn and the deductions cap's first full effect; the paper does not mention the cap in the wiki summary, so a one-line update is warranted. Its structural diagnosis (transfer-pricing opacity, uplifted deferral) is consistent with the ATO carry-forward figure and the committee's data-transparency finding.

research/total-resource-rents-australia.md uses Prosper Australia (Karl Fitzgerald, 2013; Tier 2 advocacy) figures for 2010-11 (PRRT 'effective 3.2%' for Woodside and Santos; $20.2bn EBITDAX base); these are 15 years old and Tier 2, and are now superseded for current PRRT performance by the ATO series. Derived cross-check: 2023-24 PRRT of about $1.5bn on $46.18bn assessable receipts is about 3.2%, a coincidence of ratios rather than a corroboration (different measures).
suggested_enrichment_sentences: research/australia-mining-royalties-prrt.md, PRRT section: replace 'effective 1 July 2024' with: 'The deductions cap, enacted in 2024 as Schedule 5 of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Accountability and Fairness) Act 2024, applies from 1 July 2023: for a qualifying LNG project, deductions are limited to 90% of assessable receipts, so the entity is treated as having a taxable profit of 10% of receipts in years when deductions would otherwise cut PRRT to zero; disallowed deductions are carried forward and uplifted at the long-term bond rate.' (A-claim; ATO PRRT deductions-cap and new-legislation pages.)

same page, new 'Recent revenue' paragraph: 'ATO transparency data show PRRT payable of $1.87 billion in 2024-25 across 21 entities, up 26.3% on 2023-24 ($1,483.3 million, 16 entities) despite lower oil prices, which the ATO attributes mainly to entities paying under the deductions cap. Budget cash receipts differ in timing and measure: $1.42 billion in 2024-25, with $1.4 billion estimated for 2025-26 and $1.9 billion for 2026-27 (Budget Paper No. 1, 2026-27, Table 5.7). LNG export earnings were about $65 billion in 2024-25 (Office of the Chief Economist).' Derived and labelled as such: PRRT is therefore a low single-digit percentage of LNG export earnings, with the caveat that PRRT also covers non-LNG petroleum.' (A-claims; leave the ratio out if T1 does not want a derived number.)

same page, '2026 Update' (extend the Kraal paragraph): 'A Senate select committee on the taxation of gas resources (March-May 2026) received over 230 submissions but could not agree recommendations; it found that the lack of timely, entity-level data makes PRRT liabilities hard to assess. The Greens and independent senator David Pocock urged a 25% levy on gas export revenue, Labor senators asked Treasury or the Productivity Commission to report and model reform options, and the Coalition senators stressed investment and trading-partner risk. The ATO told the committee that carried-forward PRRT expenditure stood at $282.6 billion at 2023-24. The Budget of 12 May 2026 contained no gas export tax. Revenue estimates for the 25% levy (about $17 billion a year) come from consultancy modelling commissioned by the Future Group and from the Australia Institute, not from the Parliamentary Budget Office or Treasury.' (A-claims for committee/ATO/Budget facts; the $17bn is Tier 2 and attributed.)

same page, Relation to the Georgist Case (D-claim, analysis): a flat 25% levy on export revenue is a revenue-based, royalty-type instrument rather than a tax on rent; the profit-based alternatives in the debate (a super-profits tax, a full cash-flow tax) are closer to rent taxes. Treasury told the committee that, with exports sold on long-term or global spot prices, the burden of an export levy would more likely fall on producers than on buyers (committee Hansard, quoted in additional comments).

research/nassios-australia-lng-prrt-structural-limits.md (Nuances and Limits): 'The paper's A$2.3 billion 2023 PRRT figure uses a different measure from the ATO's payable series ($1.87 billion in 2022-23); the ATO series reaches $1.87 billion again in 2024-25 after the deductions cap took effect.' (Check Nassios's data note before publishing.)

uncertainties: The 'first PRRT payment by Chevron in 2025' and the Santos/Ichthys zero-corporate-tax claims were not re-pulled from the ATO entity-level transparency tables (the 2024-25 PRRT page itself is aggregate-only).

Three official measures of 2024-25 PRRT disagree because they measure different things: ATO payable $1.87bn, Budget cash receipts $1.42bn, AEP/ABC about $1.3bn. T1 should state the measure each time and not mix them.

ATO evidence quotes (assessable receipts $46.18bn; carry-forward $282.6bn) were read second-hand in Greens, Labor and Pocock additional comments to the Senate report; Hansard (22 April 2026) and the ATO's answers to questions on notice (received 1 May 2026) were not fetched. Pocock's and the Greens' statements are Tier 3 for their own opinions but reproduce official evidence.

The Parliamentary Library $15.165bn reconciliation is cited only via Pocock; the Library paper itself was not located, and no Parliamentary Budget Office costing of a 25% export tax was found in any fetched document (searches also returned none). Treat the $17bn a year as an advocacy-commissioned estimate until an official costing is located.

Several figures in web-search summaries (for example '$108 billion' LNG earnings, and a '2026-27 Budget' 90% cap measure) conflicted with the primaries or conflate the 2023 cap with later budgets; only primary-document readings are used above.

The Treasury 2023 Review of PRRT Gas Transfer Pricing Arrangements and the Callaghan Review (2017) were not fetched; the August 2024 government statement on implementing reforms is cited in the committee comments only.

The ABC article is dated 29 April 2026, before the 7 May report and the 12 May Budget, so its forward statements ('next month's budget', 'this financial year') are superseded by the Budget figures above.
